seoDescription: Learn the complete, step-by-step process for staining a deck to preserve and protect your wood from the elements. This guide covers everything from initial preparation to final application, whether you're working with a new deck or restoring an old one. Discover how to properly pressure wash, apply deck cleaner, sand the surface for optimal adhesion, and choose the right stain—including water-based vs. oil-based options. Get professional tips on application techniques using brushes and pads for a flawless, long-lasting finish.

summary:
## Is It Time to Stain Your Deck?

To check if your deck needs a new coat of sealant, perform a simple **water test**. Pour water onto a high-traffic area:

*   **If the water absorbs immediately**, the wood is unprotected and it's time to stain and seal.
*   **If the water beads up** on the surface, your current sealant is still working.

## The Three-Step Staining Process

1.  **Preparation**: Remove old coatings and debris.
2.  **Cleaning**: Use a specialized cleaner to remove deep-seated dirt.
3.  **Staining**: Apply the new stain and sealer.

## Step 1: Deck Preparation

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Proper preparation is the most critical phase. If the surface isn't prepared correctly, the stain will not adhere properly and may peel, wasting your effort.

*   **Pressure Washing**: Use a pressure washer to remove loose stain, dirt, and mildew. 
    *   **Use a fan tip** to avoid gouging the wood, especially on softwoods like pine or cedar.
    *   Always test your technique in an inconspicuous area first.
*   **Deep Cleaning**: After pressure washing, use a chemical **deck cleaner**.
    *   It penetrates the wood to lift remaining dirt and brightens the surface for even stain absorption.
    *   Wear **protective eyewear, gloves, and closed-toe shoes**.
    *   Apply with a pump sprayer and use a **stiff-bristle brush** to work it into the grain, keeping the surface wet but not puddled.
*   **Rinsing & Drying**: After letting the cleaner sit per instructions (typically 10-15 minutes), thoroughly rinse the deck.
    *   The deck must dry for at least **48 hours** before staining. Plan your project around a clear weather forecast.
*   **Final Sanding**: Once dry, lightly sand the entire deck with **120-grit sandpaper** on a pole sander. This removes any "fuzz" raised by the pressure washer and ensures a smooth surface. Use a blower to remove all sawdust.
*   **Inspect & Repair**: Before staining, tighten loose screws and replace any damaged boards.

## Step 2: Choosing and Applying Stain

*   **Stain Selection**:
    *   **Oil-Based**: Deeper penetration, potentially longer-lasting.
    *   **Water-Based**: Easier cleanup, lower odor. Often rain-ready faster.
    *   **Semi-Transparent**: Allows the natural wood grain to show through while adding color.
*   **Application Tools**:
    *   **Brush**: Best for cutting in edges, railings, and hard-to-reach areas.
    *   **Roller**: Good for porous, older decks that need to absorb a lot of stain.
    *   **Stain Applicator Pad**: A great choice for smooth surfaces; less splatter than a roller.

> [!TIP]
> Always stir your stain thoroughly before you start and each time you refill your tray. The color pigments can settle at the bottom.

*   **Application Technique**:
    1.  Work in a team if possible: one person **cuts in** edges with a brush.
    2.  The second person follows with the main **applicator**, pulling in long, even strokes.
    3.  Plan your path to **avoid staining yourself into a corner**. Start against the house and work your way out and off the deck.

## Step 3: Cleanup and Safety

> [!IMPORTANT]
> ### Spontaneous Combustion Warning
> Rags soaked with oil-based stains can generate heat as they dry. If piled together, the combination of heat, oxygen, and cloth can cause them to spontaneously combust and start a fire. 
> **To dispose of oily rags safely, hang them individually to dry completely before throwing them in the trash.**
transcription:
## Introduction: Why and When to Stain a Deck

Sun, rain, and all the elements can take a major toll on your deck. Applying a sealant or stain not only looks great but also helps preserve and protect it. I'm gonna walk you through the step-by-step process of how to stain a deck the right way. Whether you have a new deck or are restoring an old one, you'll be ready to tackle this project in no time.

Staining a deck is basically a three-part process: remove any old stain or coatings, clean the wood, and stain and seal it. If you have an older deck and you're unsure of whether or not it's time to refinish it, here's a little trick for you. Pour some water onto a well-traveled area of the deck. If the water absorbs immediately, then you can and probably should stain and reseal the deck. 

Now, I have another freshly sealed board here, and you'll see that when I pour the water onto this board, the water is sitting on the surface. It's beading up. This is exactly what stain and sealant does for your deck: seals it and protects it.

## Prep Part 1: Pressure Washing

Alright, the first step is going to be preparation. This is not an area to skimp, guys. If you do not properly prepare your deck surface, it won't take the stain or sealant. It won't adhere and all of your work will go to waste. 

We're dealing with an older deck. It has a lot of dirt and debris on the surface that we need to get rid of. This has been well-loved, it's been stained in the past, it's had various sealants on it, so our first step is going to be pressure washing the deck.

My contractor John is helping to pressure wash this deck so that we can remove any stain, dirt, debris, and mildew that's accumulated over the years. Follow the manufacturer's instructions and recommendation for the distance the spray tip should be from the deck. A fan tip is the best choice to avoid gouging and damaging the wood. Softwoods like pine, spruce, or cedar are the easiest to damage. It's a great idea to test any pressure washing in an inconspicuous area of the deck before jumping right in.

## Prep Part 2: Applying Chemical Deck Cleaner

Okay, the next step in our preparation is thoroughly cleaning the deck. We've rinsed it off with the pressure washer and that was step one, but now we need to use a deck cleaner that's really going to penetrate into the boards and bring up dirt that's not just on the surface. This is super important to make sure that your stain or sealant adheres to your deck. If you were to skip this step you could end up with peeling and not a long-term finish. We're also applying a fresh coat of paint, so we've put tape around the base of our railings and along the edges of the house. 

Now you could kind of almost think of this process like washing dishes. If you have a dish, first you're gonna rinse it off to get everything off the surface. Then you're gonna use some soap, which is gonna cut down on the grime, and then you're gonna rinse it off again. So there's a ton of different options when it comes to deck cleaner, and you'll want to kind of pay attention to your specific wood type in your situation to choose the best one for you. 

What are we going with? So this is an Olympic wood prep cleaner. This is going to be perfect for an application like this. Even though we already pressure washed and we got a lot of the dirt and debris, there's still a little bit that's left in there and this is really gonna help pull out the rest of the dirt. The other thing it's going to do is it's going to kind of brighten. So it's gonna give us a nice surface for applying new stain.

Even though it's a simple, light cleaning product, it is pretty potent. You're going to want to make sure that you're taking extra precaution with safety. So we need to make sure that we have protective eyewear, gloves, and also closed-toed shoes.

We're applying our deck cleaner using a pump sprayer and we're pouring our cleaner directly in. We checked our package instructions and we don't need to dilute it or add anything to it at all. So we're just gonna fill it up about halfway. These are super simple to use. Basically once you put the pump back on, you're just gonna tighten that up and then you're going to pump this almost like you would a bike tire. You start feeling a little bit of resistance after probably, I don't know, I'm gonna call it like 30 pumps or so. And once you start feeling that resistance then you just lock it back into place and then you'll feel the pressure build up in here.

Alright, so John is going to spray and I am actually going to be following him back-brushing. The brush that we're using is not a broom, it might look like it, but this is a stiff bristle brush that's intended to be used for cleaning or an application, not a broom. We'll probably work on like five to ten boards at a time. It's really important that your deck cleaner stays wet, so you work in small areas. 

Basically, the goal is you want to keep the spray nozzle low to the ground so that way we're not splashing up on the paint. And then the other thing that we're doing is long, steady strokes and we're putting just enough on there to keep it wet for about 10 to 15 minutes. And what I'm gonna do is come back over it and really work the cleaner into the boards. I'm also gonna make sure that there's no puddled areas. You don't want it to be so wet that's puddling on the surface. So with the back brushing, I'm not trying to actually do the cleaning, I'm just trying to make sure that the cleaner is down into any grooves and really work it into the boards. You don't expect it to actually look any different, I just want to make sure that we have good coverage.

## Rinsing, Drying, and Final Sanding

Okay, so we finished applying cleaner to a section of about ten boards. They've had ten to fifteen minutes to sit, as per our instructions. Make sure you check your particular label. And now John's rinsing that area off. Once your entire deck is cleaned and rinsed, you're gonna need to let it dry for 48 hours. So no walking on it, keep everyone off of it, let it completely dry out. This means you're really gonna want to watch the weather. You want to plan this project for a time when there's no rain in the forecast for at least 48 hours or more. So in the meantime, I have another project planned to work on in this backyard. Over the next two days, I'm going to be building a privacy screen and you can check out that video right here, but thanks to the magic of video editing you don't actually have to wait two days to see the next step in this process. So let's get staining.

Alright, we've waited two days and our deck is fully dried. We've checked the weather and we don't have any rain in the forecast for the next two days. As you can see, this deck is looking awesome. The cleaner did exactly what we wanted it to. It's a much more even surface, it's lighter, it's brighter. 

There's a couple things we still need to do, though. John is sanding the entire deck down with some 120 grit sandpaper and a pole sander. This is gonna do a couple of things. This is gonna knock down and get rid of any debris and dirt that may have landed on the deck over the last two days while it was drying. Also, whenever you use a power washer, it can kind of open up the grain of the wood and give you almost like a little fuzz appearance to the top layer. So this pole sander will knock that down and we'll have a pristine surface ready for some stain. 

After sanding the deck, we're using a blower to get rid of all the sawdust, any debris, and make sure our deck is ready to go. Now is a great time to inspect your deck for any damaged boards. This deck's in really great condition. We only have a couple raised screws and a few loose boards, but we're gonna take care of those right now. If your deck has more damage or any boards that you need to replace, you definitely want to do that before you start to stain.

## How to Choose and Prepare Your Stain

Water-based products usually offer easier cleanup and lower odor, whereas oil-based products offer a bit of a deeper penetration and may be slightly longer lasting. Semi-transparent stains are subtle and show the grain and texture of the wood. For this deck, I'm using a semi-transparent stain plus sealer. It's water-based. It also has one-coat coverage, so we won't have to come back and do a second coat. What I also like about this one is that it's rain-ready in four hours. Even though we've checked our forecast and we know there's no rain in the forecast for the next two days, if a surprise shower would pop up, it would be okay just four hours after application. Since this product is a stain plus a sealer, when I apply it to the deck, it's going to change the color and also protect it all in one step.

We're also applying a fresh coat of paint. We've put tape around the base of our railings and along the edges of the house so we don't get any stain on them.

All right, so we're pretty much ready to get started. First thing we're gonna do is put a drop cloth down. It's really important when you're opening your stain that you don't get any stray drips on your fresh deck surface. It could leave a mark. So we're gonna open up our can of stain and it's super important with stain that you mix it, especially a semi-transparent. The tint and the color will all sink down to the bottom. So we're gonna use a stir stick. You want to make sure that you stir it very well when you're first starting and then anytime that you're refilling your tray, because again, the tint might settle down towards the bottom.

Now, for application methods, there's a few different ones you can choose, and really it's all preference. So we're gonna be using a brush for the edges. Brushes are great for any tricky, hard-to-reach areas and working your way around the whole perimeter, especially also good for around like your deck posts or anything like that. Some people like to use a roller method, so a roller on an extension pole. That works too. We're gonna be using a stain applicator, and we kind of like this one a little bit better than the roller because occasionally the roller can spit off a little bit and you might have a little bit of splatter. But if you have an older deck that's really porous and maybe needs to absorb a little more, the roller might be your better bet. For a smooth deck like this one, one gallon of stain will cover between 300 and 400 square feet. This deck is approximately 290, so we are good to go with just one can.

## Staining Technique: Cutting In and Application

Alright, we are ready to get staining and one little tip is that stain, well, it stains. So I recommend wearing some good gloves so that you don't get any on your skin. We're gonna tag-team this a bit. John is gonna work his way around the edges for me, almost like painting when you cut in the edges first. I'm gonna follow right behind him with the applicator and pull it straight from there.

So you want to make sure your brush has enough material in it. What we're gonna do is we're gonna go in about two inches and you'll see that I've got enough material, but almost too much because I'm dripping. So I'm just gonna run it along the outside of the can and that way as I'm coming across our deck, I'm not getting globs and drips on our deck. So we're gonna work it into the cracks and then we're going to also work it back into the house with the brush. That way when we come through with the applicator pad, we have a nice transition between the two. 

So now I can start following behind using the applicator in the extension pole, and you're pulling it towards you in long, even strokes. The edge of the stain applicator is actually angled, fits down into the cracks and the grooves really nicely to get the edges. Now, if you start getting inconsistent coverage like that, you know it's time to reload your applicator.

Here's a tip you'll thank me for later: you definitely don't want to stain yourself back into a corner. So in our case, we started up against the house, we're working our way out, down the stairs, and off the deck. You don't want to ever be walking on an area that you've recently stained.

## Safety, Cleanup, and the Finished Deck

One important word of caution about your cleanup: many stain products contain oil. As oily rags begin to dry, heat is produced. If they're thrown into a pile, oxygen can get trapped underneath. The combination of heat, oxygen, and cloth can lead to spontaneous combustion, which could result in a fire that could destroy your home. Make sure to let any rags hang out to dry before throwing them in the trash.

All right, we're all done staining and this deck looks brand new. Now remember, you need to check your specific product for recommendations for dry time and when you can start walking on it again. Hopefully you guys feel like you learned a ton throughout this entire process and you're confident to stain your own deck and do it right. Want to learn more? Be sure to check out the Lowe's YouTube channel for great step-by-step and how-to videos and lowes.com/howto for all kinds of projects.
